claims.text: Corrosion resistance in steels designed for chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications is primarily controlled by a continuous, self-healing Cr2O3 passive film.
Maintaining chromium above a critical threshold of approximately 12 wt% promotes formation of a stable Cr2O3 barrier.
The stable chromium oxide barrier retards ingress of corrosive species.
The chromium oxide barrier withstands aggressive chemical exposures.
The chromium oxide barrier withstands radiation environments relevant to nuclear power.
The proposed structural mediator is a continuous, adherent Cr2O3 film on the steel surface.
The Cr2O3 film limits transport of chloride ions into the steel.
The Cr2O3 film limits transport of oxygen into the steel.
The Cr2O3 film self-heals under chemical attack.
The Cr2O3 film self-heals under radiation exposure.
Maintaining the integrity of the Cr2O3 film minimizes corrosion initiation and propagation.
Maintaining the Cr2O3 film suppresses pitting corrosion.
Maintaining the Cr2O3 film suppresses intergranular attack.
Steels containing more than 12 wt% Cr will have lower corrosion rates than steels containing less than 12 wt% Cr.
High-chromium steels will exhibit less corrosion-related weight loss than low-chromium steels.
High-chromium steels will exhibit fewer localized corrosion defects than low-chromium steels.
High-chromium steels will exhibit higher electrochemical impedance than low-chromium steels.
The predicted corrosion-resistance advantage of high-chromium steels will persist under simulated nuclear radiation.
The hypothesis is expected to apply only when the passive film is not mechanically abraded or disrupted.
The protective film is expected to remain stable over chemical-processing temperatures below 150°C and nuclear-power temperatures up to approximately 400°C.
